coreTruths.title: Not every missing tooth needs replacing; the shortened dental arch is often functionally adequate
coreTruths.broaderContext: Patients arrive expecting a gap to be filled. Sometimes the right answer is to leave it alone, because the cost of intervening outweighs the gain in function or aesthetics.
coreTruths.body:
## Twenty-one teeth, including second-premolar to second-premolar contact, is usually enough

The rough threshold for a functioning dentition is twenty-one teeth or more, though the patient's age, pattern of loss, and incisal relationship modify that [1]. An occlusion with second premolar to second premolar in each arch is usually functionally adequate on its own [2]. Most dentate UK adults already sit above the threshold [3].

## Weigh the wins of replacement against its costs before committing

Better mastication, speech, occlusal stability, and aesthetics on one side. More plaque stagnation, tooth preparation, and cost on the other [2]. If the gains do not clearly outweigh the costs, replacement is contraindicated [2]. The cleanest decision is often the one not to drill anything.

## When replacement is indicated, lean minimally invasive first

A minimally invasive approach is preferable where possible [1]. Bonding techniques and implants exist precisely to avoid grinding down healthy tooth tissue [4]. A resin-bonded cantilever or an implant should be on the table before a conventional bridge that destroys tooth structure on two abutments [5].

citations.quote: Solutions for missing teeth will vary depending on the number, their location and function, and the patient’s wishes. A minimally invasive approach is preferable where possible. Twenty-one or more is considered the minimum number of teeth consistent with a functioning dentition but this may vary depending on the patient’s age, pattern of tooth loss, and incisal relationship.

First consider whether benefits of replacing missing teeth (improved mastication, speech, occlusal stability, and aesthetics) outweigh disadvantages (↑ oral stagnation, tooth preparation, cost). If not, then replacement is C/I. An occlusion with the second premolar to the second premolar present in each jaw (shortened dental arch) is usually functionally adequate.
The Adult Dental Health Survey in 2009 showed that 86% of dentate adults had 21 or more natural teeth but this proportion ↓ significantly as age i.

For those with insufficient teeth for satisfactory function and aesthetics, fixed or removable prosthodontic solutions will be needed. The use of bonding techniques and implants can help minimize unnecessary destruction of valuable tooth tissue.
Resin-bonded cantilever design is minimally invasive. Conventional bridges can have good appearance, but are destructive of tooth tissue, moderately expensive, and require lengthy clinical time.

coreTruths.title: Bridge abutment selection rests on retention and support of the tooth, not on Ante's law
coreTruths.broaderContext: The old rule that abutment root area must equal what is being replaced has no scientific basis. Abutment fitness is judged on actual retention, support, and biomechanics.
coreTruths.body:
## Retention comes from clinical crown height and surface area

Retention from a potential abutment depends on clinical crown height and the available surface area, so larger teeth beat smaller ones [1]. For resin-bonded work the question becomes how much enamel is there to bond to [1]. Full-coverage crowns and three-quarter crowns are the only retainer designs reliable enough for routine major-retainer use; onlays and inlays should sit only as minor retainers in fixed-movable designs [2].

## Support is crown-root ratio, root form, and PDL area, not Ante's law

Three things drive support. Crown-root ratio (ideally 2:3, 1:1 acceptable), root configuration (splayed beats fused), and the periodontal surface area in bone [3]. Ante's law, that abutment PDL area must match the teeth replaced, has no scientific basis and no longer has a place in contemporary bridge design [4]. The biology adapts. As load on the abutment rises, biofeedback dampens it [4].

## Pier abutments and tilted molars need design tricks, not stubbornness

A pier abutment in a fixed-fixed bridge becomes a fulcrum, and loading one end unseats the other retainer [5]. Either break the stress with a fixed-movable joint or simplify the design [5]. Tilted molars get fixed orthodontically, joined with a movable connector, or handled with telescopic crowns or precision attachments [6].

## A canine abutment forces a change in occlusal scheme

The canine is the keystone, hard to replace, and the adjacent teeth offer poor retention and support [7]. If a canine is replaced with a bridge, the occlusal scheme must be designed for group function in lateral excursion, never canine guidance [7].

citations.quote: Retention offered by a potential abutment tooth depends on clinical crown height and the available surface area. It is important to assess the amount of enamel present for retention for resin-bonded bridges. Obviously, larger teeth offer more retention and should be chosen in preference to smaller ones.

All of these restorations have been used as retainers in conventional bridgework. They are listed in order from most retentive to least retentive. Wherever possible, one of the first two should be used, as the failure rate of the last three is much higher. Post crowns should be avoided if possible, and onlays or inlays should only ever be used as minor retainers in fixed–movable bridges.
Crown–root ratio. Ideally should be 2:3 but 1:1 is acceptable. As bone is lost, the lever effect on the supporting tissues is i.

Periodontal surface area. Ante’s law, ‘the combined periodontal area of the abutment teeth must be at least as great as that of the teeth being replaced’, has no scientific basis and no longer has a place in contemporary bridgework design. It does not take into account that we are dealing with a biological system—as the load is ↑ on the abutment teeth, a biofeedback mechanism operates to cause a reduction in this load.

This is the central abutment in a complex bridge that supports pontics on either side, which are in turn anchored to the terminal abutments. In this situation, the pier abutment can act as a fulcrum and when one part of the bridge is loaded the retainer at the other end experiences an unseating force which can lead to cementation failure. To overcome this a stress-breaking element must be introduced, e.g. fixed–movable joint, or avoid pier abutments by simplifying the design.

Occurs most commonly following loss of a molar. There are several approaches if bridgework is planned: Orthodontic Rx to upright abutments. Two-part bridge, e.g. fixed–movable. Telescopic crowns—placement of individual gold shell crowns on abutments, over which the telescopic sleeves of the bridge fit. Precision attachments—a precision screw and screw tube can be incorporated into a two-part bridge.

The canine is often the keystone of the arch, and a very difficult tooth to replace. The adjacent teeth are poor in terms of the amount of retention and support that they offer and the canine is often subject to enormous stresses in lateral excursion (in a canine-guided occlusion). If a canine is to be replaced with a bridge, the occlusal scheme should be designed to provide group function in lateral excursion—never canine guidance.

coreTruths.title: Resin-bonded bridges work best as cantilevers, because fixed-fixed designs hide debonded retainers under caries
coreTruths.broaderContext: Adhesive bridgework lets a single missing tooth be replaced with almost no preparation. The trick is choosing the design that fails safely when the bond eventually fatigues.
coreTruths.body:
## Cantilever design is the safe default

Resin-bonded bridges are now used almost exclusively for cantilever adhesive bridgework, one abutment plus one pontic [1]. Fixed-fixed designs have a habit of debonding at one retainer and trapping caries underneath, undetected, until the wing finally lifts [2]. Unilateral debond is the classic failure mode, and it is why fixed-fixed adhesive bridges are no longer the norm [3].

## Maximise enamel coverage and chemical retention to a sandblasted metal wing

The modern technique relies on chemical retention to a sandblasted non-precious alloy, bonded with a dual-affinity cement such as Panavia 21 [4]. Tooth preparation should usually stay confined to enamel, with the framework designed for maximal coverage to multiply the surface area available for bonding [5]. A wrap-around design that covers more than 180 degrees of tooth circumference resists lateral displacement and reduces stress on the cement bond [6].

## Get axial loading and a 2 mm connector

Load has to travel down the long axis of the abutment. That means a cingulum or occlusal rest [7]. Connector height of at least 2 mm is required to keep the framework stiff enough not to flex and pop the bond [7]. Cementation has to happen under rubber dam, with OxyGuard over the cement to stop oxygen inhibition of the surface layer [8].

## Indications are short span, sound abutment, favourable occlusion

The sweet spot is a single-tooth space, sound or minimally restored abutments with enough crown height for bonding, and an occlusion that does not load the wing in lateral excursion [9].

citations.quote: This technique involves bonding a cast metal framework, carrying the pontic tooth, to abutment teeth using an adhesive resin. This type of bridge is almost exclusively used for cantilever adhesive bridgework, i.e. one abutment and one pontic (Fig. 7.2). Fixed–fixed designs have been problematic, with one retainer debonding being a common clinical finding.

The design is usually cantilever. If a fixed–fixed design is used and there is a debond of one retainer, caries can develop quickly and undetected under this retainer. Fixed–fixed design may be used if periodontal splinting is required or retention required following orthodontics.

Debonds. If one flange only, can usually detach other by a sharp tap with a chisel or by using ultrasonic scaler tips. If a persistent problem, consider conventional bridge. The trend is for these bridges to be used for cantilevered bridgework and it is not usual for fixed–fixed adhesive bridgework to be prescribed due to problems with unilateral debonding.
Chemical retention to a sandblasted metal surface is now used virtually exclusively. A dual-affinity cement (e.g. Panavia™ 21) is used, which chemically bonds to both enamel and non-precious alloys.
NB: tooth preparation should usually be confined to enamel, and the framework should be designed with maximal coverage (to ↑ surface area available for bonding).
↑ retention, e.g. using a wrap-around design (covering >180° of tooth circumference) to resist lateral displacement and reduce stress on the cement bond.
Provide axial loading of the abutments—prepare cingulum or occlusal rests. A connector height of at least 2mm is required.

Contamination of the fitting surface with saliva must be avoided and cementation is best done under a rubber dam. Following etching and washing of the abutment(s), and placement of a dentine adhesive system, the wings of the bridge are coated with Panavia™ 21 and the bridge seated into place and held firmly until set. Use of acetate strips and Super Floss® at this stage will clear most of the excess cement and prevent it adhering to the adjacent teeth. The cement must then be covered with a substance known as OxyGuard®, which prevents O2 inhibition of the surface layer.
Short span-single tooth edentulous space. Sound abutment teeth (or only minimal restoration) and sufficient crown height to ensure sufficient surface area for acid etch bonding. Favourable occlusion.

coreTruths.title: Partial denture design is built from support, retention, bracing, reciprocation, and indirect retention
coreTruths.broaderContext: RPDs that ignore biomechanics damage the teeth they sit on. Each of the five design principles answers a specific destructive force the denture has to neutralise.
coreTruths.body:
## Plan support before retention

Support is resistance to vertical forces toward the mucosa, and it should come from teeth wherever possible [1]. Tooth-borne support via occlusal and cingulum rests holds up better than mucosa-borne support, because teeth tolerate occlusal load and resorb less than ridges do [2]. Tissue-only support sits less harmfully in the upper arch than the lower because of the palatal vault [2].

## Three clasps as far apart as possible, plus guide planes

Direct retention usually comes from clasps; the best arrangement is three of them as far away from each other as possible [3]. Guide planes only need to be 2 to 3 mm long but they sharpen the path of insertion and reduce reliance on clasps [3]. The clasp engaging an undercut must be balanced by a reciprocal arm or a reciprocal clasp passing along a guiding plane, otherwise lateral force on the abutment goes unopposed [4].

## Match clasp material to undercut depth

The stiffer the wire, the smaller the undercut it can engage without distorting [5]. The clinical rule of thumb: 0.25 mm undercut for cast cobalt-chrome, 0.5 mm for stainless steel wire, up to 0.75 mm for wrought gold [6]. Cobalt-chrome clasps need a minimum length of 14 mm to avoid rapid distortion [7].

## Indirect retention stops the denture rocking around the direct retainers

Indirect retention places components on the opposite side of the fulcrum axis from a displacing force, so the denture cannot rotate [8]. It matters most with free-end and large anterior saddles [3].

## Lower bilateral free-end saddles need extra cunning

Kennedy Class I lowers fight a lack of distal support, small saddle area, and distal leverage on the abutment that worsens with resorption [9]. Mesial rests with a lingual plate maximise indirect retention [10]. The RPI system (mesial rest, distal guiding plate, mid-buccal I bar) is the textbook answer: under load the saddle rotates around the mesial rest while the plate and I bar disengage, sparing the abutment [11].

citations.quote: Support Resistance to vertical forces directed towards mucosa.

Plan support. Support can be tooth only, mucosa only, or both. Tooth-borne support (occlusal and cingulum rests) should be used wherever possible, as teeth are better able to withstand occlusal loading and support will not be compromised following resorption. Tooth and mucosa support are inevitable with large or free-end saddles and where plate designs are used. Tissue-only support should be utilized when no suitable teeth are available, and is less damaging in the upper than the lower arch, because of the palatal vault.

Direct. E.g. clasps, guide planes, soft tissue undercuts, or precision attachments. Of these, clasps are the most commonly used. The best arrangement is to use three clasps as far away from each other as possible. Guide planes help to establish a precise path of insertion and withdrawal. Need be only 2–3mm in length, reducing reliance on clasps. Composite resin can be added to abutment teeth to maximize undercuts.
Reciprocation The mechanism by which lateral forces generated by a retentive clasp passing over a height of contour are counterbalanced by a reciprocal clasp passing along a reciprocal guiding plane.

The stiffer the wire, the smaller the undercut that can be engaged. This can be offset by reducing the diameter of the wire to ↑ flexibility (but ↑ the likelihood of #) or by ↑ the length of the clasp arm (e.g. gingivally approaching clasp).
Depth of undercut: 0.25mm—cast cobalt–chrome; 0.5mm—SS wire; <0.75mm—wrought gold.
A minimum length of 14mm is generally advocated for cobalt–chrome clasps to prevent rapid distortion.

Indirect. This is derived by placing components so as to resist ‘rocking’ of the denture around direct retainers, e.g. by the position of clasps and rests and the type of connector. Particularly important with free-end and large anterior saddles.

This presents a particular problem because of a lack of tooth support and retention distally, small saddle area compared to force applied, and distal leverage on abutment tooth in function (which ↑ with resorption).
Maximize indirect retention by placing rests and clasps on mesial aspect of the abutment tooth and using lingual plate design.

RPI system for distal abutment teeth—mesial Rest, distal guiding Plate, and mid-buccal I bar. During function the saddle moves tissue-ward and rotates around the mesial rest. The plate and I bar are constructed in such a way as to disengage from the tooth and avoid potentially harmful loading.

coreTruths.title: Complete-denture retention and stability are different problems with different solutions
coreTruths.broaderContext: Patients say a denture is loose; they usually mean different things. Sorting retention from stability points to the right fix instead of an endless reline cycle.
coreTruths.body:
## Retention is about peripheral seal, fit, and saliva

Retention is the resistance of the denture to displacement away from the tissues. It depends on peripheral seal, contact area between denture and tissues, close fit, and the viscosity and volume of saliva [1]. Neuromuscular control has more to do with stability than retention [1].

## Stability is about the neutral zone, polished surfaces, and balanced occlusion

Stability is the ability of a denture to resist displacing forces during function [2]. The teeth need to sit in the neutral zone where lip, cheek, and tongue forces balance, more important in the lower than the upper [3]. Polished surfaces should be shaped so muscle action reseats the denture [3]. The occlusion should be balanced and free from interfering contacts [3]. None of that is a peripheral-seal problem.

## Maximum extension without overextension is the master rule

Extension goes as far as the surrounding musculature will allow, no further [3]. The upper denture extends distally over the tuberosities and onto compressible tissue just anterior to the vibrating line; the lower extends the full depth and width of the lingual pouch and halfway across the retromolar pad [3]. Overextension produces a denture that is easily displaced in function [3].

## Common faults to check first

Lack of freeway space. Failure to copy what worked in the previous denture. Occlusal errors. Wrong adaptation or extension [4]. The 'loose' denture is most often one of these dressed up.

citations.quote: The resistance of a denture to displacement. It is dependent upon (i) peripheral seal, (ii) contact area between denture and tissues, (iii) close fit, and (iv) viscosity/volume of saliva. Neuromuscular control has more to do with stability than retention.
The ability of a denture to resist displacing forces during function. Influenced by forces acting on polished and occlusal surfaces, as well as the form of the supporting tissues.

Maximum extension of denture base (as far as the surrounding musculature will allow). The upper denture should extend distally over the tuberosities and onto the compressible tissue just anterior to the vibrating line on the palate. The lower denture should extend the full depth and width of the lingual pouch, and halfway across the retromolar pad. NB: over-extension will result in a denture that is easily displaced in function.
Lack of freeway space (FWS). Failure to reproduce closely enough the features of previous successful dentures. Occlusal errors. Incorrect adaptation and extension.

coreTruths.title: Vertical dimension is set by resting face height minus a 2-4 mm freeway space, recorded in retruded contact
coreTruths.broaderContext: Get vertical dimension wrong and the patient gets soreness, cheek-biting, or a closed bite that ages them ten years. The recipe is small and has been settled for decades.
coreTruths.body:
## Freeway space sits at 2-4 mm in most patients

Freeway space is the gap between the occlusal surfaces when the mandible is at rest. In the majority of patients it is 2-4 mm [1]. The occlusal vertical dimension for an edentulous patient is therefore resting face height minus that freeway space [1].

## Measure resting face height with a Willis gauge or spring dividers

A Willis gauge measures from the base of the nose to the underside of the chin, accurate to about plus or minus 1 mm [2]. Spring dividers between dots on chin and nose tip work too, just not for bearded patients [3]. Cross-check against the patient's appearance and speech [4].

## Record the horizontal jaw relationship in retruded contact, not intercuspal

Retruded contact is the more reproducible position; intercuspal in the natural dentition sits about 1 mm forward of it [5]. Some prosthetists adjust the finished dentures so the patient can slide comfortably between the two [5]. Position the patient with the Frankfort plane horizontal because head posture itself shifts freeway space [6].

## Set the occlusal plane between the ridges, parallel to inter-pupillary and ala-tragal lines

About 1-2 mm of upper tooth should show below the upper lip at rest, less with age [7]. The occlusal plane lies midway between the ridges and parallel to the inter-pupillary line and the ala-tragal line [7]. The tongue should rise just above the lower occlusal plane posteriorly [7].

## At fitting, vertical dimension lives in upper-palatal to lower-buccal cusp contact

Adjustment of cusps that maintain VD should be avoided where possible [8]. Use the BULL rule for lateral interferences: adjust buccal upper and lingual lower cusps only [9].

citations.quote: Vertical dimension. The FWS is the space between the occlusal surfaces of the teeth when the mandible is in the rest position. In the majority of patients it is 2–4mm. The OVD for an edentulous patient can therefore be determined by measuring their resting face height and subtracting a FWS.
A Willis gauge, to measure the distance between the base of nose and the underside of the chin. Is only accurate to ±1mm.
Spring dividers, to measure the distance between a dot placed on both the chin and the tip of the patient’s nose. This method is less popular with patients and is C/I for those with a beard.
The patient’s appearance and speech.

Horizontal jaw relationship. Record the more reproducible RCP. In the natural dentition, ICP is ~1mm forward of RCP; some prosthetists advise adjusting the finished dentures to allow the patient to slide comfortably between the two positions.
As head posture can affect FWS, position the patient so that the Frankfort plane is horizontal. A wax trimmer and a heat source are required to adjust the rims.

Position of the occlusal plane. This should be placed so that ~1–2mm (↓ with age) of tooth are visible below the patient’s upper lip at rest. The occlusal plane should lie midway between the ridges parallel to the inter-pupillary and the ala-tragal lines. At rest, the tongue should rise just above the lower occlusal plane posteriorly.
The vertical dimension of the dentures is maintained by contact between the upper palatal and lower buccal cusps, therefore adjustment of these should be avoided if possible.

For cusped teeth only, place articulating paper between occlusal surfaces and ask patient to make small lateral movements and adjust buccal upper and lower lingual (‘BULL’ rule) cusps only to remove any interferences.

coreTruths.title: Alveolar resorption is progressive; preserving roots and choosing implants reshapes long-term outcomes
coreTruths.broaderContext: Edentulous ridges shrink for the rest of the patient's life, the mandible faster than the maxilla. Every prosthodontic decision is also a bone-preservation decision.
coreTruths.body:
## Resorption keeps going, and the lower jaw loses ground faster

Resorption is progressive with time, which is itself a good argument for not rendering young patients edentulous [1]. The mandible resorbs more quickly than the maxilla, which is why retention for the lower complete denture is the harder problem [1].

## Overdentures keep roots and the bone they sit in

An overdenture takes support from one or more abutment teeth or implants by enclosing them under its fitting surface [2]. Keeping a root preserves alveolar bone around it, gives a better crown-to-root ratio that reduces lateral leverage, and preserves PDL proprioception so the patient still feels what they bite on [3]. The trade-off: the abutment usually needs RCT, the denture base may have to be thinned over the abutment which weakens it, and the roots are now caries-prone [4].

## Two implants in the edentulous mandible is the agreed minimum standard

A large body of evidence supports the proposal that a two-implant-supported mandibular overdenture should be the minimum offered to edentulous patients as a first-choice treatment [5]. Patient satisfaction and quality of life are significantly higher with implant-supported overdentures than with conventional full lowers [5].

## Plan the partial dentate transition before resorption forces the issue

In the older partially dentate patient, judge whether they are likely to keep functional teeth for life [6]. If not, some advocate providing complete dentures while the patient is still young enough to adapt [6]. Reduced adaptive capacity is the real reason: if teeth will not last a lifetime, the move to at least partial dentures should happen while the new skills can still be learnt [7]. Immediate dentures need warning the patient about resorption and early rebasing, with recall at 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, then yearly [8].

citations.quote: Resorption is progressive with time, which is a good argument for avoiding rendering young patients edentulous. The mandible resorbs more quickly than the maxilla, which exacerbates the problem of retention for −/F.
An overdenture (OD) derives support from one or more abutment teeth or implants by completely enclosing them beneath its fitting surface. It can be a partial or complete denture.

Alveolar bone preservation around the retained tooth. Improved retention, stability, and support. Preservation of proprioception via PDL. Better crown-to-root ratio, which ↓ damaging lateral forces. ↑ masticatory force.

RCT probably required. To avoid excessive bulk in region of retained tooth (which may compromise aesthetics), denture base may need to be thinned, which ↑ likelihood of #. ↑ maintenance for both patient and dentist. Roots may be prone to caries.

There is good evidence that a patient’s satisfaction and quality of life is significantly ↑ with implant-supported ODs than with conventional full dentures. The York Consensus Statement on implant-supported ODs states that ‘a large body of evidence supports the proposal that a two-implant-supported mandibular overdenture should be the minimum offered to edentulous patients as a first choice of treatment’.

In the older, partially dentate patient it is important to assess whether the patient is likely to retain some functional teeth for the remainder of their lifespan. If this is improbable, some advocate providing F/F dentures while the patient is still young enough to adapt.
Reduced adaptive capacity; therefore if teeth are unlikely to last a lifetime, the transition to at least partial dentures should be made while the patient is able to learn the new skills necessary.

Regular inspection of immediate dentures is important as rapid bone resorption means that they will require rebasing early. However, this should be deferred, if feasible, for at least 3 months after the extractions. A possible regimen is 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, and then yearly.

coreTruths.title: Denture stomatitis is a candidal-ecology problem, not a fit problem
coreTruths.broaderContext: Red palate under an upper denture is the textbook denture-wearer complaint. Trauma is not the main driver. Candida, plaque, and night-time wear are.
coreTruths.body:
## The classic picture is a red, symptomless palate under an upper full denture

Denture stomatitis is usually symptomless despite its old name of denture sore mouth. Classically: redness of the palate under a full upper, with petechial and whitish areas [1]. About 90 percent of cases are Candida albicans, 9 percent other Candida species, and under 1 percent other organisms [1]. It has been reported in 30-60 percent of complete-denture wearers [2].

## Trauma is not the primary driver

Trauma gets blamed but the picture does not fit. The condition is more common under upper than lower full dentures, can affect patients with only an upper, and is also seen under well-fitting orthodontic appliances [3]. The drivers that actually correlate are Candida infection, poor denture hygiene, and night-time wear [4].

## Management is hygiene, night-off, and only then antifungals

First-line: take the dentures out at night, brush the fitting surface, soak in hypochlorite, reduce sugar [5]. The denture itself can act as a Candida reservoir, so if compliance is good and the redness persists, the denture may need replacing [6]. Miconazole gel can be applied to the fitting surface, and systemic fluconazole is reserved for selected cases [7]. Look for systemic predisposers (iron and vitamin deficiency, steroids, xerostomia, endocrine abnormalities) and refer if suspected [8].

citations.quote: Also known as denture sore mouth, a misnomer because the condition is usually symptomless. Classically, seen as redness of the palate under a F/− denture, with petechial and whitish areas. 90% of cases due to Candida albicans, 9% to other Candida spp., and <1% to other organisms, e.g. Klebsiella spp.
A common condition, having been reported in 30–60% of patients wearing F/F. It affects F more commonly than M, in a ratio of 4:1, and usually affects the upper denture-bearing area only.

Trauma is often cited as a contributing factor to denture stomatitis, but: It occurs more commonly under F/− than −/F. It can affect patients wearing F/− only. It is also found under well-fitting orthodontic appliances.
Infection with Candida spp. Poor denture hygiene. Night-time wear of dentures.
Patients should be encouraged to remove their dentures at night. They should cleanse denture thoroughly, e.g. brushing fitting surface and soaking in hypochlorite cleanser.
New dentures may be required if these measures fail despite good compliance. The denture can act as a reservoir for Candida.

Miconazole gel can be added to the fitting surface of the denture before insertion. If suspect systemic factors exacerbating condition, refer to GMP. Coexisting papillary hyperplasia of palate may need surgical reduction. Systemic fluconazole may be used in some cases.
Systemic factors can predispose to Candida infection, e.g. iron and vitamin deficiency, steroids, drugs which cause xerostomia, and endocrine abnormalities.
